sketches.title: Tiny Trial
sketches.premise: An everyday object is on trial for being only one star. You and the House each write the strangest fair case against it while keeping the card’s plain truth intact.
sketches.criterion: The move must still make the card’s fact true, while turning the object into a believable defendant without adding a false result.
sketches.move_shape: Write one under-90-character courtroom claim, witness line, or verdict; for example, card “A zipper joins two sides of cloth” → “ZIPPER ON TRIAL: Witnesses say it joins, then jams at the border.”
sketches.first_card: A pencil has a wooden body and a graphite center.

sketches.title: Manual Mishap
sketches.premise: You are writing the worst helpful instruction manual for an ordinary object. Make the instructions wildly dramatic, but a reader must still learn the card’s plain fact.
sketches.criterion: The move must preserve the card’s one fact as an instruction or warning, while the invented advice makes the object seem worthy of one star.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 90 characters as a manual step, warning, or troubleshooting tip; for example, card “A broom has bristles” → “Step 1: Use the bristles to chase crumbs into a new kingdom.”
sketches.first_card: A spoon has a bowl-shaped end for holding food.

sketches.title: Object Obituary
sketches.premise: Give an everyday object an affectionate obituary after its one-star life. The joke may blame its habits or choices, but the card’s quiet fact must remain true.
sketches.criterion: The move must retain the card’s fact inside a short obituary-style entry and may not claim the fact stopped being true.
sketches.move_shape: Write up to 90 characters as a headline, tribute, or final notice; for example, card “A clock shows the time” → “Beloved clock, remembered for showing time five minutes too late.”
sketches.first_card: A shoelace is a cord used to fasten a shoe.

sketches.title: Complaint Counter
sketches.premise: You have reached the customer-service desk for an object that earned one star. State a funny complaint and the remedy you demand, while keeping the card’s basic truth in view.
sketches.criterion: The move must keep the card’s fact true and frame the object’s failure as a clear customer complaint rather than merely describing the game.
sketches.move_shape: Write one complaint, reply, or refund demand under 90 characters; for example, card “A mug holds a drink” → “Refund requested: this mug holds tea, but not my attention.”
sketches.first_card: An umbrella is used to help keep rain off a person.

sketches.title: Museum of Misses
sketches.premise: Create a museum label for an everyday object that visitors have rated one star. The label can invent a grand history, but its displayed object must still have the card’s plain feature.
sketches.criterion: The move must describe or title an exhibit while preserving the card’s fact and making the object’s ordinary feature feel like a disappointing achievement.
sketches.move_shape: Write a museum label, exhibit title, or curator note under 90 characters; for example, card “A key opens a lock” → “EXHIBIT 4: Tiny metal hero, opening one lock since Tuesday.”
sketches.first_card: A ruler is marked with units for measuring length.

sketches.title: Reviewer Reply
sketches.premise: An everyday object has received your one-star review, and now it writes back. Answer in the object’s voice with gentle excuses, keeping the card’s plain fact true.
sketches.criterion: The move must speak as the object and preserve the card’s fact while adding a playful reason its performance deserves only one star.
sketches.move_shape: Write the object’s reply in up to 90 characters; for example, card “A towel absorbs water” → “I absorb water beautifully; returning it dry is outside my job description.”
sketches.first_card: A mirror reflects light and can show a person’s image.
